title: Canada Puts $20 Million Behind Fast Track to Ontario Licences for Foreign-Trained Doctors
excerpt: Health Canada's October 7 funding expands Practice Ready Ontario, letting experienced internationally trained physicians qualify for family medicine through a 12-week clinical assessment instead of a two-year residency.
body:
• Health Canada committed $20 million on October 7 to expand Practice Ready Ontario, a fast track that lets experienced internationally trained physicians become licensed for family medicine through a 12-week clinical assessment instead of a two-year residency.
  • The funding advances 200 internationally trained physicians and adds 50 new positions per year over four years, with all participants expected to be practising in Ontario by 2028-29.
  • To qualify, a physician must be a Canadian permanent resident or citizen, meet education, experience and language requirements, and sign a three-year return-of-service agreement to practise in Ontario, including underserved northern, rural and Francophone communities.
  • The move is the latest in a 2026 policy push — including a new federal permanent residence pathway for physicians and 14-day work permit processing — aimed at easing Canada's primary-care shortage.

Canada is accelerating a program that lets experienced foreign-trained doctors start practising family medicine in Ontario in under a year, putting $20 million behind the expansion of a clinical fast track that bypasses the traditional two-year residency.

Health Canada announced the funding on October 7 for Practice Ready Ontario (PRO), which allows internationally trained physicians — many of them Indian-educated — to become licensed to practise family medicine through a 12-week clinical field assessment. The money will advance 200 physicians along the pathway, including a dedicated stream for French-speaking doctors, and fund 50 additional positions per year over four years, with the goal of having all participants practising in Ontario by 2028–29.

How the fast track works

Under PRO, an experienced internationally trained physician can be licensed from start to finish in less than a year, compared with a typical three-to-five-year timeline through other routes. To qualify, the physician must be a Canadian permanent resident or citizen and meet minimum requirements for education, work experience and language proficiency, administered by the Touchstone Institute in collaboration with the Ontario government and the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario.

"A separate $11 million in the same announcement funds five other projects supporting licensing for internationally educated nurses, physiotherapists and occupational therapists across the country."

There is a catch: doctors licensed through PRO must sign a three-year return-of-service agreement committing to practise in Ontario. During that period they work under supervised practice, and they become fully licensed for independent practice only after completing the agreement and passing the national Certification Examination in Family Medicine.

Part of a wider 2026 push

The October 7 announcement extends a busy year of federal action on foreign-trained health workers. In December 2025, Ottawa created a dedicated federal permanent residence pathway for physicians with Canadian work experience — 891 physicians have already been invited to apply — allocated 5,000 more spaces for physicians under provincial pathways, and introduced 14-day work permit processing for province-nominated doctors. On January 1, new Ontario legislation took effect allowing physicians licensed in other provinces to be authorised to practise in Ontario in as little as two business days.

Health Canada says the expanded program will specifically improve access to primary care in underserved northern and rural regions and Francophone communities in Ontario. A separate $11 million in the same announcement funds five other projects supporting licensing for internationally educated nurses, physiotherapists and occupational therapists across the country.

Why it matters for Indian physicians

India-trained doctors are among the largest groups of internationally trained physicians in Canada, and the labyrinth of licensing requirements — often called "brain waste" — has left thousands driving taxis or working outside medicine while the country faces a chronic family-doctor shortage. PRO's 12-week assessment model directly addresses that mismatch by testing clinical readiness rather than demanding a full repeat of residency.

That said, the program is not open to newcomers abroad: eligibility requires permanent residence or citizenship, so it helps doctors already in Canada rather than creating a new immigration route. For Indian-origin physicians on the path to permanent residence, the federal physician pathway and faster provincial work permits are the doors that lead here.

What to watch

The test will be placement and retention. A three-year service commitment in underserved regions could either finally bring doctors to doctor-starved communities or simply delay the drift to big-city practices. The first cohorts through the expanded program should reach full independent licensing around 2029 — and Ottawa will be judged on whether those 200 physicians are still in family medicine, and still in Ontario, a few years later.
